header.title: The live test run, hop by hop
header.intro: `uv run pytest -m live` ran four tests on 2026-10-11 at 00:56, and authtrace captured every HTTP call the pytest process made (strict redaction). Three tours replay them: **One meme** follows the end-to-end test through Keycloak, memes-mcp and Claude; **No permission** shows a token with the right audience but no `memes:read`; **Background** shows an offline grant being redeemed, rotated, revoked and refused. memes-mcp was already running, so its side (token validation, the JWKS fetch) is explained from its code, not seen on the wire. The browser login isn't in this run.
header.diagram_alt: pytest, playing the memes-dev client, talks to Keycloak (authorization server), memes-mcp (resource server) and the Claude API. Inside pytest sit the agent loop, MCPToolGateway, ClaudeLLM, the worker and GrantStore; inside memes-mcp sit the auth middleware, the session manager and the tools. The JWKS hop from memes-mcp to Keycloak is dashed because it wasn't captured.

1: Map resource owner, client, authorization server and resource server onto running code.
2: What's inside each token, and who checks iss, aud, exp, scope and sub.
3: An MCP server built with Arcade's framework, protected as a resource server.
4: The hand-written loop: model, tools, repeat, and why the token never reaches the model.
5: Which API a token is for (aud) versus what it may do there (scope), checked per tool.
6: Refresh tokens, offline grants for the worker, rotation, revocation and re-consent.

inspector.title: Token inspector: the access token from test 1
inspector.intro: `t1`, decoded. Reading a JWT needs no key; trusting one needs the signature check in the One meme tour, step 5. Identity claims are hashed because the capture is `strict`. The right-hand columns say which code checks each claim, from memes-mcp's installed arcade-mcp-server 1.32.

claims.why: Must equal the configured algorithm before any key is used, which blocks algorithm-confusion tricks. The refresh token is HS512, so it could never pass here.
Picks the public key in Keycloak's JWKS. An unknown `kid` is a 401 until the 1-hour JWKS cache refreshes, which is why memes-mcp needs a restart after a realm re-import.
Exact string match with `http://localhost:8080/realms/memes`. A token from another realm or IdP fails.
Must contain `CANONICAL_URL`. The `memes-mcp` default client scope's audience mapper puts it there, for every token memes-dev and memes-web get.
900 s after `iat`. Validation is local, so `exp` is the only revocation memes-mcp ever sees.
Rejected if it's in the future (clock skew, leeway 0).

claims.checked_by: memes-mcp → `context.user_id`; the app's profile and grant key
claims.why: Required (no `sub`, no entry). The stable identity: never the email or username.
The middleware only parses it; the tools enforce it. Without `memes:read` the session still opens, and every tool refuses (the No permission tour).
Which client asked: `memes-dev` here, `memes-web` in the browser. A separate worker client would make background calls visible in it.
Keycloak's own marker (`Bearer`, `Refresh`, `Offline`, `ID`). memes-mcp relies on `alg` and `aud` instead to keep other token types out.
Keycloak's session id. It changes per password grant, and stays the same across the offline refresh in the Background tour.

claims.checked_by: nobody (copied into the resource owner, unused)
claims.why: Display only. Emails can change; `sub` can't.

logs_note: This page was built on 2026-10-11 from the capture in `.authtrace/run-20261011-005646/`, unchanged. Only the pytest process ran under capture; memes-mcp and Keycloak were already running.

steps.title: Get tokens the dev way: the password grant
steps.what: `dev_token()` posts the **password grant** to Keycloak as the public `memes-dev` client. It asks for `openid memes:read`. Keycloak answers with three tokens and adds `email profile`, the client's default scopes. It also applies the default `memes-mcp` scope, whose audience mapper writes `aud=http://127.0.0.1:8001/mcp`. That scope doesn't show in `scope` because it is configured with `include.in.token.scope: false`.
steps.wire:
→ POST http://localhost:8080/realms/memes/protocol/openid-connect/token
  {"grant_type": "password", "client_id": "memes-dev", "username": "…", "password": "…",
   "scope": "openid memes:read"}
← 200
  {"access_token": "<jwt fp:4b64c169>", "expires_in": 900, "refresh_expires_in": 1800,
   "refresh_token": "<jwt fp:d33f962b>", "token_type": "Bearer", "id_token": "<jwt fp:c6ce940b>",
   "scope": "openid memes:read email profile"}
checks: `memes:read` is an optional scope on memes-dev → granted on request
steps.roles: Resource owner: the realm's dev test user · Client: `memes-dev`, played by pytest · Authorization server: Keycloak realm `memes`
steps.note: Finding **OAUTH-ROPC** (x1, x15, x24, x37) is by design: `memes-dev` exists so tests and scripts can get a token without a browser, and the decision log marks it dev only. `memes-web`, the real client, has the password grant switched off and uses the authorization code flow with PKCE.
quiz: Nobody asked for the `memes-mcp` scope. Why does `aud` name the MCP server?

`memes-mcp` is a *default* client scope on memes-dev, so Keycloak always applies it, and its audience mapper adds the MCP server's canonical URL to `aud`. `include.in.token.scope: false` hides it from `scope`.

steps.title: Three tokens, three audiences; only one leaves
steps.what: The access token `t1` is for memes-mcp. The refresh token `t2` is for Keycloak itself, and the ID token `t3` is for the client. The test keeps only `t1` and hands it to `MCPToolGateway`. The capture confirms that no refresh token ever reached memes-mcp (rule **REFRESH-TO-RS** passed).
steps.wire:
t1  access   RS256  typ Bearer   aud http://127.0.0.1:8001/mcp           900 s
t2  refresh  HS512  typ Refresh  aud http://localhost:8080/realms/memes  1800 s
t3  id       RS256  typ ID       aud memes-dev                           900 s
checks: reading a JWT isn't trusting it; that happens in step 5
steps.inv: A user's identity is the Keycloak `sub`, never an email or a username.
quiz: Could someone replay the refresh token `t2` at memes-mcp?
No. It's HS512 (a secret only Keycloak holds), memes-mcp accepts only RS256 keys from the JWKS, and its `aud` is the realm, not the MCP URL. The ID token `t3` fails the `aud` check too.

steps.title: Open an MCP session: the 2026 probe gets a 400
steps.what: `MCPToolGateway` builds one HTTP client with `Authorization: Bearer …` as a default header, so *every* MCP request carries `t1`. The `mcp` 2.2 client defaults to `mode="auto"`: it first probes `server/discover` at protocol `2026-07-28`. On memes-mcp, `ResourceServerMiddleware` wraps the whole `/mcp` mount and validates the token first. Only then does the session manager compare the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header with its supported list (`2025-06-18`, `2025-11-25`) and answer 400.
steps.note: Finding **MCP-VERSION-FALLBACK** (x2, x16, x26) is expected: the decision log says a single 400 per connection is the price of the forward-compatible client. It's version negotiation, not an auth failure. A rejected token gets a **401** with `WWW-Authenticate` instead.
steps.roles: Client: pytest via `MCPToolGateway` · Resource server: memes-mcp
quiz: How do we know `t1` was valid, even though this request failed?
The middleware wraps the whole `/mcp` app. A bad token would have stopped there with a 401 and never reached the protocol-version check that produced this 400.

steps.title: Fall back to 2025-11-25: initialize, stream, tools/list
steps.what: Any error on the probe makes the client fall back to the classic `initialize` handshake, which is exempt from the version-header check. The server agrees on `2025-11-25` and names itself `Memes 0.1.0`. `notifications/initialized` (202) and a `GET` event stream complete the session, and `tools/list` returns both tools in alphabetical order, which is why the loop picks tools by name. The middleware re-validates `t1` on each of these requests.
checks: sig · iss · aud · exp, on every request
initialize negotiates the version; later requests must match it
quiz: `tools/list` showed both tools. Does that mean this token may call them?
No. Listing needs only a valid token. Each tool checks `memes:read` itself, as the No permission tour shows with a token that lists both tools and then gets refused by each.

steps.title: Validate the token: JWKS signature, iss, aud, exp
steps.what: memes-mcp configures one trusted issuer: the Keycloak realm, its `/certs` URL, `RS256`, and `expected_audiences=[CANONICAL_URL]`. For every request, the validator takes the cached JWKS (refetched after 3600 s), finds the key whose `kid` matches and whose `alg` is RS256, and verifies the signature. Then it checks `exp`, `iat` and `nbf` with zero leeway, `iss` by exact string, `aud` against the canonical URL, and that `sub` exists. It parses `scope` into `granted_scopes` but enforces nothing there. The result, a *resource owner*, rides along to the tools.
steps.wire:
t1 header  alg RS256  kid K4RimLbP…
iss == http://localhost:8080/realms/memes   ✓
aud ∋  http://127.0.0.1:8001/mcp            ✓
exp    iat + 900 s, still in the future     ✓
sub    present → context.user_id
steps.inv: The MCP server trusts only JWTs it has validated (signature, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`).
steps.note: The JWKS fetch itself isn't in this capture: memes-mcp was started before the run and wasn't wrapped, so the dashed edge stays *inferred*. Running `uv run memes-mcp` under `authtrace run` would show it (once per hour at most).
steps.roles: Resource server: memes-mcp, validating locally · Authorization server: Keycloak, only as the JWKS publisher
quiz: An admin ends this user's Keycloak session right now. Does `t1` stop working at memes-mcp?
No. Validation is local (cached keys, no call to Keycloak), so `t1` keeps working until `exp`, 15 minutes after it was issued. Short access-token lifetimes are what keep that window small.

steps.title: Claude picks a tool: only words and schemas cross
steps.what: `run_agent` puts the user's words in the first message as data, fetches the tool schemas, and calls `ClaudeLLM`, which sends only `model`, `system`, `tools` and `messages`. Claude answers with a `tool_use` block for `Memes_MakeMeme`. The capture scanned every model request for known token values; rule **TOKEN-LEAK-LLM** passed for all seven.
checks: no known token in the request → passed
its own API key, not an OAuth token
steps.inv: Tokens never reach the LLM. `MCPToolGateway` attaches them; the model sees names and arguments only.
steps.roles: Claude is not an OAuth party: it never holds the user's token and can't choose whose token is used.
quiz: Claude asked for `Memes_MakeMeme`. Could it make that call run as a different user?
No. The token was fixed when the gateway was built, and the model only supplies a tool name and arguments. Identity comes from the token's `sub`, never from arguments.

steps.title: Call Memes_MakeMeme as the user
steps.what: The loop calls `tools.call`, and the gateway sends `tools/call` with the Bearer header. After the middleware validates `t1` again, arcade sets `context.user_id` from the token's `sub`. The first line of `make_meme` is `require_scopes(context, "memes:read")`, which reads the validated scopes (through a private attribute, kept in `scopes.py`). `t1` has `memes:read`, so the tool picks a meme and returns it as `structuredContent`, which the loop keeps for the UI.
steps.inv: Every tool checks its own scopes with `require_scopes` (fail closed).
steps.roles: Resource owner: the user behind `sub` · Client: pytest via the gateway · Resource server: memes-mcp
quiz: Where does memes-mcp get the user's identity: the tool arguments or the token?
The token. `sub` becomes `context.user_id`. The arguments carry only hints, which are data, never identity.

steps.title: A caption is rejected, and Claude rewrites it
steps.what: Claude submits a caption (x9 → x10), and memes-mcp answers HTTP 200 with `isError: true` and arcade's `_meta` error block. The scope check passed (`t1` has `memes:read`), so this is `caption_meme` raising a `RetryableToolError`: either an unknown `meme_id` or a caption the PG guard rejected. The strict capture dropped the message, so which one is *unknown*. The gateway turns it into an `is_error` result, the loop hands it back to Claude, and the rewrite (x11 → x12) is approved. There's no retry code anywhere.
steps.wire:
→ tools/call Memes_CaptionMeme    ← 200 {"result": {"_meta": "…", "content": [...], "isError": true}}
→ tools/call Memes_CaptionMeme    ← 200 {"result": {"content": [...], "structuredContent": "…", "isError": false}}
checks: is_error goes back to Claude as data
steps.inv: Errors are data: tool failures go back to the model as `is_error` results.
steps.note: Run the test with `--redaction dev` to keep the rejection text and see which check fired.
quiz: Is x10 an authorization failure?
No. Auth failures look different: a 401 from the middleware, or an `insufficient_scope` error from `require_scopes`, and `t1` passes both. This is the caption gate, reported as data for the model.

steps.title: Claude finishes, and the MCP session closes
steps.what: Claude replies with text and `end_turn`, so the loop stops. Leaving `async with MCPToolGateway` closes the client, which sends `DELETE /mcp` to end the session. That request is validated too. Nothing tells Keycloak: `t1` isn't revoked, it just stops being used.
steps.wire:
→ POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages   ← 200 {"stop_reason": "end_turn"}
→ DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8001/mcp
  Authorization: Bearer <jwt fp:4b64c169>
← 200
checks: even DELETE needs a valid token
quiz: After the DELETE, could `t1` still open a new session?
Yes, until its `exp` (900 s after issue). DELETE ends the MCP session, not the token, and memes-mcp validates locally, so only `exp` limits it.

steps.title: Ask for only openid: right audience, no permission
steps.what: The scope test asks for `scope=openid` only. `memes:read` is *optional* on memes-dev, so it's left out; `memes-mcp` is *default*, so `aud` still names the MCP server. Since the 2026-10-04 split, "which API" (audience) and "what may it do" (permission) are separate scopes.
checks: default scopes applied; optional memes:read not requested
quiz: Before the split, removing `memes:read` gave a 401. Why?

The audience mapper lived on `memes:read`, so a token without it also lost `aud`, and the middleware rejected it. Now the audience comes from the default `memes-mcp` scope and the permission is separate.

steps.title: The door opens: session and tools/list succeed
steps.what: The same probe 400, then the same handshake. `t4` passes the middleware because its signature, `iss`, `aud` and `exp` are fine; scope isn't part of that check. Arcade's built-in scope enforcement runs only for tools declared with `requires_auth`, and these tools aren't. `tools/list` returns both tools, as the test asserts.
steps.wire:
→ POST /mcp server/discover   ← 400 Unsupported protocol version: 2026-07-28
→ POST /mcp initialize        ← 200 2025-11-25
→ POST /mcp tools/list        ← 200 [Memes_CaptionMeme, Memes_MakeMeme]
checks: sig · iss · aud · exp ✓ (scope not checked)
quiz: Why doesn't the server refuse `t4` at the door?
The door checks *who the token is for* (aud) and that it's genuine. *What it may do* is decided per tool, so one server can host tools with different scopes.

steps.title: Every tool refuses: insufficient_scope, as data
steps.what: Both calls reach their tools, and the first line of each, `require_scopes(context, "memes:read")`, raises `ToolExecutionError("insufficient_scope: …")`. Arcade returns that as HTTP 200 with `isError: true`, and the test asserts `insufficient_scope` in both. The spec-ideal answer is HTTP 403 with `WWW-Authenticate: insufficient_scope`, which arcade's middleware can send for `requires_auth` tools; the project chose errors as data for now. The session then ends (x23).
steps.inv: Every tool checks its own scopes with `require_scopes` (fail closed): no token, no scopes, no tool.
steps.note: The test lists every tool by name and fails on a new one that isn't listed, so a tool can't ship without a scope check.
quiz: How could a client learn which scope to ask for?
Two ways: the error names `memes:read`, and memes-mcp's protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) advertises `scopes_supported=["memes:read"]`.

steps.title: Consent once: an offline grant
steps.what: The worker test asks for `openid memes:read offline_access`. The refresh token `t8` now has `typ: Offline` and lives 604800 s (7 days idle, the realm's offline policy) instead of 1800 s. The test stores it in `GrantStore`, Fernet-encrypted, keyed by `sub`. In the app, this is the step-up consent at `/background/enable` through the browser, not a password grant.
checks: offline_access is optional on memes-dev, and the user has the role
steps.note: The access token `t7` from this grant is never used: the worker always refreshes first.
steps.roles: Resource owner: the user, consenting once · Client: memes-dev (the test) · Authorization server: Keycloak
quiz: Why is the offline token the most sensitive thing the app stores?
It survives logout and the SSO session for up to 30 days, and it mints fresh access tokens. So it's encrypted at rest and only the worker redeems it.

steps.title: The worker swaps the grant for a fresh access token
steps.what: `run_once` decrypts the grant and refreshes it *before* doing anything else. Keycloak returns a new access token `t10` and a new offline refresh token `t11` (new `jti`, same `sid`), and the worker saves `t11` before running the agent, so a crash can't lose the grant. The test's refresher uses the public `memes-dev` client, with no secret. The real worker uses `memes-web` and its client secret.
checks: offline session alive; refresh token issued to this client
asserts the stored grant changed (rotated and saved)
steps.note: This capture shows a *new* refresh token. It doesn't show the old one dying. The realm file doesn't set `revokeRefreshToken`, which Keycloak leaves off by default, so `t8` may still be redeemable. Nothing re-used it here. An opt-in probe that redeems `t8` a second time would settle it.
quiz: Lesson 6a says the grant can only be redeemed with memes-web's client secret. Does that hold in this test?

No. This grant was issued to the public `memes-dev` client, which has no secret, so the encrypted `GrantStore` is the only protection. A refresh token is bound to the client it was issued to, which is why the test can't use the real worker's refresher.

steps.title: Same agent, same checks: memes-mcp can't tell it's background
steps.what: The worker hands `t10` to a fresh `MCPToolGateway` and runs the same `run_agent`. On the wire it's test 1 again: the probe 400, the handshake, `Memes_MakeMeme`, and `Memes_CaptionMeme`, approved on the first try this time. memes-mcp validates `t10` exactly like `t1`. Same `iss`, same `aud`, same `azp`. Only `scope` adds `offline_access`. The meme goes to the inbox.
steps.wire:
→ POST /mcp server/discover          ← 400
→ initialize · initialized · GET · tools/list   ← 200 · 202 · 200 · 200
→ tools/call Memes_MakeMeme          ← 200 isError false
→ tools/call Memes_CaptionMeme       ← 200 isError false
→ DELETE /mcp                        ← 200

t10  aud http://127.0.0.1:8001/mcp  azp memes-dev  scope openid memes:read email profile offline_access
checks: sig · iss · aud · exp, same as for t1
quiz: How could memes-mcp's logs tell a background call from a click?
Today they can't: same client, same claims. The `# EXTEND:` in `worker.py` proposes a separate `memes-worker` client, so `azp` would differ. Another one down-scopes the refresh to `memes:read` only.

steps.title: Stop: revoke the grant at Keycloak
steps.what: The last test gets a new offline grant, stores it, and revokes it at Keycloak's revocation endpoint (RFC 7009), as "Stop" does. The test is a public client, so it sends only `client_id`. The app's `/background/disable` authenticates with memes-web's secret, revokes, and then deletes the row. Deleting only our copy would leave a live grant at Keycloak.
checks: the token belongs to memes-dev → offline session ended
quiz: Why revoke at Keycloak before deleting the row?
The grant lives at Keycloak as an offline session. Deleting our encrypted copy alone leaves it valid until its 7-day idle or 30-day max lifetime runs out.

steps.title: The worker finds a dead grant: invalid_grant → needs_reauth
steps.what: `run_once` tries to refresh the revoked token. Keycloak answers 400 `invalid_grant`, because the offline session behind it is gone. The worker treats that as "only the user can fix this": it marks the grant `needs_reauth`, drops the token, and moves on. The app shows a Reconnect banner. No MCP or Claude call happens; the test passes no gateway or model at all.
steps.inv: Re-consent is a product flow, not an error: a dead grant becomes `needs_reauth`, never a silent delete.
quiz: The worker catches `OAuthError` separately from other exceptions. Why?
`invalid_grant` is permanent, so retrying is pointless and the user must re-consent. A network error is temporary, so the grant is kept and retried on the next pass.

flows.name: No permission: a token without memes:read
